title: Scalable Production of Efficient Single-Atom Copper Decorated Carbon Membranes for CO2 Electroreduction to Methanol
abstract: Electrocatalytic reduction reaction of CO2 (CO2RR) is an effective way to mitigate energy and environmental issues. However, very limited catalysts are capable of converting CO2 resources into high-value products such as hydrocarbons or alcohols. Herein, we firstly propose a facile strategy to the large-scale synthesis of isolated Cu decorated through-hole carbon nanofibers (CuSAs/TCNFs). This CuSAs/TCNFs membrane has excellent mechanical properties and can be directly used as cathode for CO2RR, which could generate nearly pure methanol with 44% Faradaic efficiency in liquid phase. The self-supporting and through-hole structure of CuSAs/TCNFs greatly reduces the embed metal atoms and produce abundant efficient Cu single atoms, which could actually participate in CO2RR, eventually causing BC7 mA cm partial current density for C1 products and more than 50 h stability in aqueous solution. According to DFT calculations, Cu single atoms possess a relatively higher binding energy for *CO intermediate. Therefore, *CO could be further reduced to products like methanol, instead of being easily released from the catalyst surface as CO product. This report may benefit the design of efficient and high-yield single-atom catalysts for other electrocatalytic reaction.

sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
CO2 is not only the major greenhouse gas, but also a cheap, clean and abundant C1 resource. Developing a cost-effective process for
the electrochemical CO2RR could achieve a shift in chemical industry and sustainable energy economy.1-2 Coupled to a
renewable energy source like wind or solar, electrochemical
CO2RR is a candidate for electrical energy storage from intermittent renewable sources into stable compounds as well.3
Since CO2RR is a kinetically slow and diverging reaction that requires efficient catalysts.4 The key technological challenge to
achieve such a procedure is developing a kind of active and
selective catalysts, i.e. proper catalysts that can transform CO2 molecules into desirable products at relatively high current densities and hold out long enough.1 Unfortunately, the most
common products of CO2RR from the many electrocatalysts previously investigated are CO and formate,1, 5-6 which are not as
easy to use as fuels like hydrocarbons or alcohols.
Among currently identified materials, Cu is the only recognized
material catalyzing the production of a large number of hydrocarbons or alcohols in aqueous solutions.6-13 However, Cu-
based electrocatalysts usually generate a fairly broad mix of
gaseous and liquid phase chemicals. Controlling the catalytic
selectivity of CO2RR to desired product remains a significant challenge.4 This poor selectivity might be attributed to the various
lattice planes, defects or vacancies of polycrystalline and oxidized
Cu, which could exhibit fundamentally different efficiency or selectivity in CO2 electroreduction,14 i.e. Cu(100) surface tend to ethylene formation at relatively low overpotential, while Cu(211)
surface can produce significant amounts of methane but only less amount of ethylene.15 Moreover, CO2RR in aqueous solution occurs at the three-phase interface, therefore the adsorption of CO2
molecules and the desorption of corresponding products on the
catalyst surface represent a crucial step dictating the efficiency of catalysts.8 Hence, the catalytic activity of CO2RR electrocatalysts is mainly determined by the surface active sites while the
contribution of internal atoms is very limited. Consequently,
completely exposing and unifying the status of the copper element
is a approach to better selectivity and efficiency for electrochemical
CO2RR. Anchored metal single atom (M-N-C) material might be an ideal choice to satisfy these demands, due to their unique electronic structure and maximized atomic utilization.16 Recent
reports have shown that M-N-C (like Co/Ni/Fe/Mn-N-C) materials were indeed outstanding electrocatalysts for CO2RR,17-25 i.e. A-NiNSG catalysts could reduce CO2 to CO with nearly 100% selectivity.19 Unfortunately, M-N-C electrocatalysts have only
produced the two electron reduction products of CO and formate so
far. There are few reports on the further reduction of CO2 to hydrocarbons or alcohols catalyzed by M-N-C materials, to the best
of our knowledge. Besides, most of the M-N-C catalysts are
powder-based and specific polymer binders are necessary to make
them useful as working electrodes. During powdering and binding
procedure, massive single atoms would be embedded inside the
polymer binders and cannot exhibit catalytic activity in CO2RR. The existence of extensive inefficient metal atoms is not in
accordance with maximized atomic utilization principle of
single-atom catalysts.
Herein, we design a facile procedure to synthesize through-hole
carbon nanofibers (TCNFs) with abundant and homogenously
distributed Cu single atoms (CuSAs) for the efficient
electrochemical CO2RR with high stability. Notably, Cu as well as their mixtures or oxidized forms have been demonstrated to be the most effective materials for the CO2 electroreduction to methanol.911 Hence, with the synergetic interaction of the through-hole carbon

sections.heading: MATERIALS AND METHODS
sections.text:
This section describes only the key experimental methods.
Detailed materials and methods are described in Electronic
Supporting Information.
Synthesis of CuSAs/TCNFs Catalyst. Firstly, 1.8 g polyacrylonitrile (PAN, Mw=130000) powder was dissolved in 20
mL N,N-Dimethylformamide (DMF) in a three-neck bottle by
magnetically stirring to obtain a homogenous solution. Then, 0.6 g
of Cu/ZIF-8 nanoparticles were added in the PAN/DMF mixed
solution and the compound was magnetically stirred to yield a
homogenous precursor solution. The precursor solution was firstly
moved into a syringe with a stainless needle at the tip, which is
linked to a high voltage power equipment, and then electrospun to
polymer fiber by a parallel-plate apparatus. The as-spun nanofibers
were carbonized under Ar at 900 °C for 1 hour, and the heating rate
is 5 °C/min from room temperature (about 20 °C) after a pre-
oxidated procedure in air at 220 °C for 1 hour. After cooled to room
temperature under Ar, the resultants were washed thoroughly in a
4.0 M H2SO4 aqueous solution for 10 hours to remove Cu nanoparticles (if exist) and the residual Zn species. After drying in vacuum at 60 oC overnight, CuSAs/TCNFs was thus obtained.
Materials and Instruments. All chemicals were commercially purchased and utilized as received.
Linear sweep voltammograms (LSV) were recorded with
electrochemical work-station (Princeton Applied Research 263A).
Potentiostatic electrolysis were performed via a CHI 660C
electrochemical station (Shanghai Chenhua). Liquid reduction products were detected via 1H and 13C NMR spectra using an
Ascend 400 spectrometer (500 MHz, Bruker). Liquid-phase
reduction products were detected by Gas Chromatography (SRI
8610C). Field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM)
pictures were taken with FEI JEOL-7800F. Transmission electron
microscopy (TEM) images and element mapping analysis (EDS)
were recorded on JEM-2100F field emission electron microscope.
The high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron
microscopy (HAADF-STEM) analysis was carried out on a JEOL
JEM-ARF200F TEM/STEM equipped with a spherical aberration
corrector. N2 adsorption-desorption was conducted at 77 K using a Micromeritics ASAP 2460 instrument with degassing samples
under vacuum at 573 K for 10 h. The X-ray absorption find
structure (XAFS, Cu K-edge) spectra were conducted at 1W1B
station of Beijing Synchrotron Radiation Facility. The storage rings
of Beijing Synchrotron Radiation Facility was carried out at 2.5
GeV with a maximum current of 250 mA. The data were acquired
in transmission mode using ionization chamber using Si(111)
double-crystal monochromator. All the mentioned spectra were
performed under ambient conditions.

sections.heading: RESULTS
sections.text:
Synthesis and Characterization of CuSAs/TCNFs
Catalysts. The synthetic strategy for CuSAs/TCNFs is briefly depicted in Scheme 1a. Firstly, ZIF-8 nanoparticles (Figure S1)
was uniformly dispersed in n-hexane, and then the Cu(NO3)2 aqueous solution was injected into the as-prepared mixture above
for the adsorption of Cu ions. Through this double-solvent method,
Cu ions would be restricted in the pores of ZIF-8, leading to the
formation of Cu/ZIF-8 nanoparticles. Then, these Cu/ZIF-8
nanoparticles were embedded into PAN nanofibers by an
electrospinning method, which would be transformed into N-doped
carbon nanofibers in following carbonization procedure. The adsorbed Cu2+ ions would be reduced by adjacent carbon species
and some of them would be successfully anchored by N and form
the isolated Cu atoms via the Lewis acid-base interactions between
Cu-N coordination. Cu nanoparticles might also emerge because of
the accumulation of Cu atoms. Then the remaining Zn species or
Cu nanoparticles were completely etched by H2SO4 solution. This flexible and self-supported CuSAs/TCNFs could be obtained ~310 square centimeters (Figure S2, Scheme 1b) under laboratory
conditions. The CuSAs/TCNFs can maintain its sheet structure
under bending stress sometimes (Scheme 1b), manifesting the
comparable strength and flexibility with carbon cloth and can
tolerate approximately 1 MPa tensile strength in stress-strain test
(Figure S3).

As shown in FE-SEM (Figure 1a, b and Figure S4) and HR-
TEM (Figure 1c, d and Figure S4) images, the tightly aligned
carbon nanofibers of CuSAs/TCNFs form interconnected network
structure with a diameter of ca.700 nm. In addition, the through
nanoholes on the CuSAs/TCNFs were directly seen using both FE-
SEM and HR-TEM (Figure 1b-d and Figure S4). These
nanoholes show an uniform pore size of ca. 100 nm, similar to the
size of Cu/ZIF-8 nanoparticles. If the amount of Cu(NO3)2 keeping unchanged but ZIF-8 nanoparticles dropping to one-third of
CuSAs/TCNFs, the holes significantly declined and tended to be
disconnected and embedded within carbon nanofibers (Figure S5),
which was entitled as CuSAs/CNFs. On the contrary, through-hole
structure still exists in carbon nanofibers of TCNFs (Figure S6)
when the same amount of ZIF-8 (without adsorption of Cu ions)
was added in electrospinning solution, indicating that the formation
of nanoholes is attributed to ZIF-8 nanoparticles. N2 adsorptiondesorption test was measured to further examine the porous
structure of CuSAs/TCNFs. The nitrogen adsorption-desorption
curve of CuSAs/TCNFs showed an isotherm with both type-I and
type-IV properties, manifesting the hierarchical porous structure of
CuSAs/TCNFs (Figure S7a-b). The specific surface area of CuSAs/TCNFs membrane was up to 618 m2 gB- on basis of multi-
point BET method (Table S1). Pore size distribution curve
indicated that the pore size mostly distributed at ~100 nm,
corresponding to the observation from SEM and TEM patterns.
TCNFs has the similar through-hole structure as CuSAs/TCNFs
(Figure S8). However, N2 adsorption-desorption curve of CuSAs/CNFs only shows microporous structure (Figure S7c-d),

embedded in graphene nanosheet were investigated as the activity
center of CuSAs/TCNFs, while Ni-N4 and pyridine N doped graphene nanosheet were also introduced as contrast (Figure 4b
and Figure S18). The adsorption and reaction free energies of key intermediates and steps12 in CO2 electroreduction on the above systems were calculated (Table S4).
The as-proposed reaction paths of CO2 reduction as well as free energies of all the systems are manifested in Figure 4a and Figure
4c. According to the DFT calculations, the conversion of CO2 molecule to adsorbed COOH* is the rate determining step (RDS), since the free energy patterns of three systems are all uphill type.3035 Especially, Ni-N4 structure shows the most advantageous freeenergies (0.98 eV) for RDS, followed by Cu-N4 (1.17 eV), and pyridine N (1.62 eV). Then, the as-generated COOH* intermediate
can be easily converted to a CO* species for all three samples along
with a proton and an electron. For Ni-N4 (-0.21 eV) and pyridine N (-0.54 eV), the CO* desorption step both exhibit negative free-
energies, revealing that the CO* intermediate can be efficiently eliminated from the catalyst surface and lead to CO products.36 In
contrast, the *CO desorption on Cu-N4 has a slightly positive freeenergy (0.12 eV), indicating a endergonic step. Therefore *CO
intermediate can be furtherly reduced to methanol rather than being easily released as CO.7, 37-41
It also notable that only C1 chemicals (CH3OH and CO) were found in the gaseous and liquid products from CO2 reduction, and no C2+ products were detected. Typically, C2+ products (e.g.
C2H4, C2H6 or C2H5OH) were obtained from the dimerization (or C C coupling) of specific C1 intermediates (like *CO) with a high local concentration4, 42. Since the Cu element mostly presents as
atomically-dispersed sites in our CuSAs/TCNFs catalyst, the B
coupling route of these *CO intermediates into advanced products
is substantially blocked, causing the enhancement of CO and
CH3OH production in our experiments. On one hand, some researchers have predicted that Cu-based single-atom catalysts
could electrocatalyze CO2 into CH3OH using first-principles calculations very recently.43 On the other hand, as C1 chemicals,
CH4 is another potential product from CO2 electroreduction on single-atomically dispersed Cu sites.

To further explore the reaction mechanism of CH3OH and CH4 on our CuSAs/TCNFs catalyst, we complete the DFT calculations
from *CO to methanol. The calculation model (Figure S19) and
reaction pathways for CH3OH (1) and CH4 (2) formation were proposed based on our research and former reports.9, 43-47 To
produce CH3OH, the *COH intermediate should be reduced to *CHOH rather than *C, which is key step for CH4 formation. According to DFT calculations (Figure 5), the reduction of COH*
to CHOH* on Cu-N4 structure has a moderate free energy barrier
( 0.86 eV). In contrast, the step of COH* to C* shows much higher
free energy barrier ( 1.88 eV), which is also higher than any steps
in CH3OH production. Therefore, the single-atom Cu sites on CuSAs/TCNFs catalyst tend to generate CH3OH instead of CH4.

sections.heading: CONCLUSION
sections.text:
In summary, we develop a facile method for the rational design
and facile synthesis of highly stable and efficient through-hole
carbon nanofibers decorated with abundant and homogenously
distributed Cu single atoms. The CuSAs/TCNFs can be directly
used as cathode for CO2RR due to the excellent mechanical properties. With the synergetic effect of the through-hole carbon
structure and abundant isolated Cu active sites, CuSAs/TCNFs exhibits 44% Faradaic efficiency and BC7 mA cmB6 partial current
density of methanol as well as long-term stability. CuSAs/TCNFs
membrane is easily massively produced according to the
standardized step, which would fulfill the industrial production
requirements.
